ledger.sentence: Spirometry is the most common lung function test.
ledger.note: Retrieved review text calls spirometry the most commonly used lung function test (non-UK academic source).

ledger.sentence: It measures how much air a person can blow out and how quickly.
ledger.note: Retrieved text: spirometry measures how much and how fast air can be exhaled; lung volumes need a separate lung volume test.

ledger.sentence: Spirometry is the main test for detecting airflow obstruction, while other lung function tests measure lung volumes and gas exchange.
ledger.note: Retrieved: spirometry is the main test for airflow obstruction; wider lung function tests assess lung volumes and gas exchange. Wording 'capacity ... how clear airways' not found.

ledger.sentence: The person wears a nose clip so air goes through the mouth, and breathes through a mouthpiece into the lung function machine.
ledger.note: Retrieved: nose clip or holding the nose, lips sealed around mouthpiece.

ledger.sentence: They breathe normally, take a deep breath in, and then blow out as hard and fast as possible.
ledger.note: Retrieved: deep breath in, then a forceful, fast breath out until the lungs feel empty.

ledger.sentence: Each blow may be repeated several times, with rests in between.
ledger.note: 'At least three times' not found in retrieved text; one source says you may have to repeat the manoeuvre a number of times.

ledger.sentence: One NHS trust says the test normally takes around 15 minutes.
ledger.note: One NHS trust leaflet: the whole test normally takes around 15 minutes; others say 10 to 30 minutes.

ledger.sentence: One NHS practice suggests avoiding vigorous exercise for 30 minutes before the test.
ledger.note: Retrieved NHS sources: avoid vigorous exercise for about 30 minutes before.

ledger.sentence: The same guidance suggests wearing loose clothing.
ledger.note: Loose clothing retrieved; dentures, chewing gum and bladder not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: It also notes that a recent chest infection, or recent antibiotics or steroids, can affect the results.
ledger.note: Retrieved: recent antibiotics or steroids can affect results; recent coughing up blood or surgery can make testing unsuitable. 'Heart attack in last three months' not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: Preparation varies, and patients are told whether they need to stop any inhalers or medicines beforehand.
ledger.note: Retrieved: stopping times for inhalers vary by drug and patients are told if they need to stop medicines; 'appointment letter' not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: The test is sometimes repeated after a reliever inhaler to check whether it helps the airways.
ledger.note: Retrieved: the repeat-after-inhaler test is sometimes done to investigate asthma or when the diagnosis is unclear, not always 'often'.

ledger.sentence: The person takes the test, uses the inhaler, waits a short time and repeats the test.
ledger.note: Retrieved: spirometry, then inhaler, a pause (10 to 40 minutes depending on the trust and medicine), then repeat.

ledger.sentence: The comparison shows how much the airways respond to the medicine, and the test is sometimes used when asthma is being investigated.
ledger.note: Retrieved: the comparison shows how much airways respond to medicine and helps check whether the inhaler helps breathing. 'Supports a diagnosis of asthma' not retrieved; NICE says a single normal result does not rule out asthma.

ledger.sentence: Results are compared with predicted values for someone of the same height, age and sex.
ledger.note: Cornwall NHS guideline: predicted values are calculated from height, age and sex.

ledger.sentence: A typical report shows the measured values alongside the predicted values.
ledger.note: Retrieved: a typical report shows measured values, predicted values and percent predicted; 'reference values used' not specifically retrieved.

ledger.sentence: In obstructive conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways narrow, making it harder for air to flow out of the lungs.
ledger.note: StatPearls/PMC: obstructive diseases raise resistance to airflow through partial or complete airway blockage; spirometry diagnoses asthma and COPD.

ledger.sentence: Restrictive conditions are different, because they decrease the amount of air the lungs can hold.
ledger.note: StatPearls: restrictive disorders have smaller lung volumes, mainly lower total lung capacity.

ledger.sentence: One NHS leaflet says results are discussed at the next clinic appointment with the consultant or GP.
ledger.note: Royal Wolverhampton leaflet: results are discussed at the next clinic appointment with the consultant or GP. 'Respiratory doctor arranges follow-up' not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: NHS leaflets describe the test as painless and non-invasive, with dizziness or fainting the most common side effects and more serious complications very rare.
ledger.note: Retrieved NHS leaflets mention dizziness or fainting, and rare serious complications (airway narrowing, collapsed lung); not 'no risks'.

ledger.sentence: The test needs a good effort, which can make some people feel dizzy or faint.
ledger.note: Retrieved: exertion required can cause dizziness or fainting; 'tiring' and recovery time not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: Some people feel dizzy or faint, and coughing is common.
ledger.note: Retrieved: some patients feel dizzy or faint; coughing is common.

ledger.sentence: In spirometry the person breathes through a mouthpiece, with a nose clip, into a machine that measures airflow.
ledger.note: Nose clip and mouthpiece into a spirometer (retrieved).

ledger.sentence: The test may be repeated after a reliever inhaler to see whether it helps breathing.
ledger.note: Retrieved: sometimes repeated after an inhaler to see whether it helps breathing.
